Meningitis Fungal diseases associated with meningitis include as- pergillosis, candidiasis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococco- sis, and histoplasmosis (see above), although many dis- seminated fungal infections can involve the CNS, especially in immunocompromised patients. The treat- ment of each infection is discussed under the appropriate heading, but in general the initial drug of choice in fungal meningitis is intravenous amphotericin B, sometimes with flucytosine. Mucormycosis Mucormycosis,1-5 a rare but invasive and rapidly progres- sive infection caused by Mucorales fungi, is a form of zy- gomycosis, a term that is sometimes used synonymously. Mucormycosis usually acquired by inhalation of spores, although trauma and ingestion may also be routes of infec- tion. It usually occurs in poorly controlled diabetic patients or in immunocompromised patients. Patients given desfer- rioxamine may also be at increased risk of infection (see p.1440). Infections of the mucosa of the respiratory tract or gastrointestinal tract, or of abraded skin, usually with Rhiz- opus or Rhizomucor spp., can result in local invasion of deeper tissues including bone and the CNS, with extensive tissue destruction. Disseminated disease may also occur. The treatment of mucormycosis includes a combination of antifungal therapy, surgical debridement when possible, and management of the underlying disease. The standard antifungal therapy is relatively high doses of intravenous amphotericin B or lipid formulations
